output.headline: Netanyahu to ‘highlight Israel’s achievements’ in UN speech as protests and a walkout are planned
output.standfirst: Prime minister, in growing political isolation and facing protests and a planned walkout, heads towards his toughest re-election challenge; envoy says speech will ‘highlight Israel’s achievements’
output.bodyHtml:
Benjamin Netanyahu will take the stage at the UN on Thursday to deliver a familiar message of defiance, in a speech his ambassador says will set out ‘what still should be done’ – even as protests and international condemnation leave the Israeli leader in growing isolation.

The speech comes as Netanyahu faces the toughest re-election challenge of a political career spanning decades, with three ongoing conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran and a growing campaign of violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank.

Internationally, the UK, France and Canada are planning to sanction Israeli settlements in the West Bank, part of growing condemnation of Israel, and the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has accused Israeli settlers of committing ethnic cleansing of Palestinian communities.

In the US, public opinion is in the midst of a historic shift against Israel: 62% of respondents told Pew in July they had a negative opinion of Netanyahu’s government, and 60% of American Jews in a poll released this week hope he is voted out in October.

New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, assured demonstrators this week that he would protect their “right to [protest] in this city”, tempering his earlier promises to arrest Netanyahu as a war criminal, as protests are expected both in the UN’s general assembly hall and on the city’s streets.

Speaking in a telephone interview before this week’s speech, Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, defended Netanyahu’s government and sought to cast criticism of Israel’s actions as the product of misinformation and bias.

“We are aware of the fact that we had a very challenging three years since October 7,” Danon said. “We accomplished a lot, but we were criticised. We were under the spotlight, and for us, I think, we are proud of our achievements.”

He added: “At the same time, we will work harder to improve the image of Israel, and we know there’s a campaign against us.”

Organisers have scheduled several protests in New York City on Thursday, where anger at Netanyahu will be on full display, including one from Bryant Park in midtown Manhattan to the UN headquarters in Turtle Bay to “reject war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu and the genocidal Zionist project”.

Beth Miller, the political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, said: “Netanyahu is coming to New York amid a political environment that has made it crystal clear that he is not welcome here.”

She described a “mainstreaming” of the public view that “Americans do not want to be supporting Israel’s genocide. We do not want to be supporting Israel’s apartheid. We do not want to be arming Israel or supporting Israel.”

Palestinian representatives, meanwhile, are calling for diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”.

Netanyahu would use his speech to “highlight Israel’s achievements”, Danon said, and to lay out “what still should be done, and how should we verify that we actually achieve the goals of the war?” In Danon’s telling, Israel’s problem was largely one of public relations rather than of policy, and he cited a “wave of misinformation” as the reason for the precipitous shift in polling.

The White House and US policymakers will be listening as they calibrate their message to voters – as well as the backlash of public anger – ahead of the upcoming midterm elections, though Danon did not elaborate on those specific measures before the speech.

The hardline message Netanyahu is expected to deliver is aimed not just at world leaders but also at his own electorate in Israel ahead of the October elections. Miller said: “I think that he is trying to demonstrate to the Israeli populace that he still maintains some level of control over the situation. And I think that he is trying to speak to a rightwing audience and a Trump-Maga audience in this country to try to rile up the hatred and Islamophobia.”

The visit is expected to last less than 24 hours, and Donald Trump and top US officials are not expected to meet with Netanyahu during it. Trump will be in Washington DC to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, while Netanyahu has cited Israel’s electoral campaign and the holiday of Sukkot as his reason to head home quickly after the speech.

Netanyahu’s delegation had sought a high-level meeting during the visit, a Trump administration official said, but none was organised. Nor are there plans to meet congressional leaders, Danon said.

Top Republicans, including the vice-president, JD Vance, and leading Democratic presidential contenders have both voiced criticism, meaning Israel could face a 2028 campaign with two candidates who no longer support arms sales to Israel or the broad diplomatic support that it has enjoyed in the past.

Miller noted fractures even within the Maga base, with “more and more people who don’t really want to be sending our tax dollars to support the Israeli government”.

Of a potential shift in the US-Israeli security relationship, Danon said: “I think that we are still sharing the same values, and that’s why I’m sure that we will continue to have the support from the US.”

There are now multiple flashpoints for anger from both US political parties and from the international community, however, including dire humanitarian concerns and the lack of reconstruction in Gaza, the expansion of settlements in the West Bank and continued conflicts in Lebanon and Iran, where the US has found itself mired in a conflict that has driven up global energy prices.

Danon pointed to efforts by the Trump-backed Board of Peace when asked whether a controversial $2.8bn (£2.1bn) arms sale indicated that Israel is preparing to resume its offensive in Gaza, saying Israel “hopes that we will see [Hamas’s] disarmament without our involvement”. If that does not change, he said, Israel “will do it ourselves”, adding: “We can not leave it forever like that.”

On the West Bank he was equally resolute, saying that Israel would not be swayed by recent criticism led by the UK over plans to expand settlements including E1, the planned construction which would sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank.

Senate Democrats are also introducing a bill on Wednesday to sanction facilitators of the new settlement. Senator Chris Coons, a co-sponsor, said in a statement that “as Palestinian civilians face a campaign of devastation and fear from violent extremist settlers, the United States must send a strong message that this behaviour is unacceptable”.

The protests began before Netanyahu had even arrived in New York.

Several members of the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter rallied on Wednesday at the city’s John F Kennedy international airport, protesting at weapons and explosive materials destined for the Israeli military being flown out of the airport on commercial aircraft.

Among the speakers was Aber Kawas, who in November is slated to become the first Palestinian-American elected official in New York state. She later told the Guardian she plans to join many other New Yorkers protesting against Netanyahu’s UN speech on Thursday.

“Thousands of people are against his presence in our city,” she said.

Some had hailed Netanyahu’s decision to cut his visit short as a victory, she added, but “the fact that he is coming shows he continues to have a sense of entitlement to be centred on the world stage while being the head architect of a genocide”.
